name: Meta Ads & Pixel Blueprints
tagline: Whether your budget can work at all, first
oneLiner: The tracking code, the event map, the campaign structure — and the arithmetic that decides whether any of it can work at the budget you actually have.
audience: Anyone about to spend their first $500 on Meta ads
Agencies running client ads without a documented event map
Sellers whose Pixel fires on every page and measures nothing
problem: Paid traffic fails at small budgets in a way nobody warns about: the campaign never gathers enough conversion events to leave the learning phase, so the algorithm optimises on noise and the money goes out in a straight line. That is arithmetic, and it can be checked before the first cedi is spent — but almost every guide starts with campaign structure and never mentions it.
solves: Spending a budget too small to exit the learning phase
A Pixel installed but no event map, so nothing is optimisable
Campaign structures copied from a video with different economics
No idea what a conversion may cost before it stops making sense
inside: The tracking setup: Pixel and Conversions API, with what each one is actually for
An event map derived from your funnel, not a generic list of standard events
Campaign structure per objective, with the budget each structure needs
The learning-phase arithmetic: events per week required, at your conversion rate
Maximum allowable cost per acquisition from your own margin
A verdict that is allowed to say your budget cannot work yet
outcomes: A yes or no on paid traffic at your current budget and margin
An event map you can hand to whoever installs the code
A campaign structure with a budget that matches it
usage: Open index.html and enter your margin and conversion rate first.
Read the learning-phase verdict before designing anything. If it says the budget is too small, that is the most valuable output here.
Build the event map from your real funnel steps.
Take the tracking spec to whoever installs it — it is written to be handed over.
Set up campaigns to the structure, and hold the budget it specifies.
notFor: Anyone wanting creative or copy — this is measurement and structure
Advertisers with large budgets and an in-house analyst
proof: It has no access to your ad account and cannot see your results. Everything is computed from figures you enter, and the thresholds are stated on screen.

name: SEO & Content Marketing Systems
tagline: Not how many search it — whether writing it pays
oneLiner: Keyword selection, clustering, internal linking and structured data, plus the arithmetic that says whether a content programme ever repays what it costs.
audience: Anyone whose blog has forty posts and no traffic
Agencies selling content retainers they cannot justify with numbers
Founders deciding between SEO and paid
problem: Keyword tools answer how many people search a phrase and leave the only question that matters to you: would writing it ever pay you back. So content marketing fails in a predictable way — the articles get written, they are perfectly good, they rank on page four, and eighteen months later nobody can say whether the programme made or lost money.
solves: Keywords chosen by search volume, which is the wrong variable on its own
Articles written as isolated posts with no cluster or internal linking
No structured data, so the pages compete without the features that win clicks
A content budget with no payback model behind it
inside: Keyword selection scored on intent, difficulty and what a click is worth to you
Clustering — the pillar and its supporting articles, planned as one unit
An internal linking map that ships with the cluster
Structured data per article type, written out
Article briefs detailed enough to hand to a writer or a model
Payback arithmetic: cost per article against the traffic and value it must earn
outcomes: A ranked keyword list where the ranking accounts for what a visitor is worth
Clusters planned before writing, not discovered afterwards
The month the programme breaks even, computed from your own costs
usage: Open index.html and enter what a conversion is worth to you. Everything downstream needs it.
Score your candidate keywords; ignore the volume column on its own.
Build one cluster completely before writing a second pillar.
Generate the briefs and the linking map together.
Check the payback model before committing to a monthly output.
notFor: Anyone wanting live keyword data — it makes no network requests, so the volumes are yours to supply
Sites needing technical SEO audits of existing code
proof: It cannot see the SERP. It structures and computes; the search data has to come from you, from whatever tool you already use.

name: Email Marketing Automation
tagline: What to send, and what a subscriber is worth
oneLiner: A calendar, a launch sequence, subscriber value arithmetic, and the model of what mailing everyone does to the people who still read you.
audience: Anyone told to 'build a list' and left there
Sellers with a list they are afraid to email
Creators whose open rate is falling and cannot see why
problem: 'Build a list' is advice that stops exactly where the work starts. Nothing in it says what to put in the emails, how often to send, what a subscriber is actually worth, or what mailing everyone every week does to the people who still open — which is the mechanism by which lists quietly die while the subscriber count goes up.
solves: A list that never gets emailed because there is no plan for what to say
Sending to everyone every time and burning the engaged segment
No idea what a subscriber is worth, so no idea what acquiring one may cost
Launch sequences improvised the week of the launch
inside: A send calendar with the cadence your list size and content supply can sustain
The launch sequence: seven emails over ten days, each with its job
A lead-magnet design that recruits buyers rather than freebie collectors
Subscriber value arithmetic — what one is worth, so acquisition has a ceiling
Segment fatigue modelling: what full-list sending does to your openers
Drafting prompts built from each email's own brief
outcomes: A publishing cadence you can hold for a quarter
A launch sequence written before launch week
A number for what a subscriber is worth, and therefore what one may cost
usage: Open index.html and set list size, open rate and what a customer is worth.
Read the subscriber value figure before you plan any acquisition spend.
Build the calendar around what you can genuinely produce.
Write the launch sequence in advance and store it.
Check the fatigue model before any full-list send.
notFor: Sending the emails — no ESP is connected; you paste into yours
proof: Every figure comes from your inputs. Deliverability depends on your sending platform and your history, neither of which this can see.

name: Social Media Content Automation
tagline: The calendar your week can actually produce
oneLiner: Reconciles what you promised to post, what your source material can yield, and how many hours you have — before week three empties the calendar.
audience: Anyone whose content calendar is half empty by week three
Agencies promising posting volumes they then cannot staff
Creators repurposing one video into 'twenty pieces of content' in theory
problem: A content plan is allowed to contain three contradictory numbers: what you promised to post, what your source material can actually yield, and how many hours exist. Nothing in the usual planning process forces them to agree, so the calendar is arithmetically impossible on the day it is written — and everyone blames discipline in week three.
solves: Posting schedules that were never producible
Repurposing claims that do not survive contact with the source material
Production hours nobody counted
A queue that empties silently and takes reach with it
inside: The three-number reconciliation: promise, yield, hours — with the shortfall named
Realistic repurposing ratios per source type
A production system with batching, so a week's posts are made in one session
A calendar that refuses to schedule more than your inputs support
Per-platform format specs so one asset is not remade five times
The rescue plan for a queue that has already run dry
outcomes: A calendar that can survive the month it was written for
The honest number of posts your source material yields
A batching session that replaces daily scrambling
usage: Open index.html and enter your posting promise, your source material and your real weekly hours.
Read the shortfall. Fix it by lowering the promise or raising the input — not by resolving to try harder.
Set the repurposing ratios to what you have actually achieved before.
Batch-produce against the calendar in one session per week.
Re-run the reconciliation whenever you take on a new channel.
notFor: Scheduling or publishing — it plans, it does not post
Anyone wanting the content written for them
proof: The reconciliation only works with honest hours. Optimistic input produces an optimistic calendar and the same empty week three.

name: The Faceless YouTube Toolkits
tagline: Six tools for an eighteen-month game
oneLiner: Niche scoring out of 21, a ten-step production workflow with its prompts, a Shorts strategy, a five-layer monetisation stack and the month-by-month income curve.
audience: Anyone starting a faceless channel
Creators three months in and wondering whether the curve is normal
People choosing a niche by what they like watching
problem: Content at scale is the hardest income stream to act on, because everything in it is a long game: a niche test, a production workflow, a Shorts strategy, a monetisation stack, an income curve that takes eighteen months to resolve. All of it arrives as prose you read once and then have to remember for a year and a half.
solves: Choosing a niche by interest rather than by RPM and durability
A production process re-invented per video, so video four takes as long as video one
Monetisation left entirely to ad revenue
Quitting at month five because nobody said what month five looks like
inside: Niche Scorecard — seven criteria out of 21, with the RPM band attached
A ten-step production workflow that fills in its own prompts
A Shorts strategy that feeds the long-form channel rather than replacing it
The five-layer monetisation stack, calculated on your figures
A weekly schedule you can actually hold alongside a job
The month-by-month income curve, with a marker for which row you are on today
outcomes: A niche chosen on scores you can defend in month nine
A repeatable production run instead of a per-video adventure
A realistic view of when money appears, so month five is not a surprise
usage: Open index.html and score three candidate niches before choosing one.
Run the production workflow for your first video and time each step.
Set up the monetisation stack early; ad revenue alone is the slowest layer.
Keep the weekly schedule visible.
Check the income curve monthly to see whether you are on, above or below the expected row.
notFor: Anyone wanting videos produced for them
Channels already monetised and looking for platform-specific optimisation
proof: The income curve is a documented model, not a promise. Your channel will differ; the value is in knowing what normal looks like before you panic.

name: AI Website Prompt Kit
tagline: Decide it, or the builder decides it for you
oneLiner: Works out what an AI site builder must be told before the first message, writes the prompts from your answers, and prices what the missing answers cost in redos.
audience: Anyone building a site with an AI builder or a chat model
Freelancers producing client sites and re-prompting for hours
People on their third purple-gradient hero
problem: An AI website builder never asks for what it was not given. Say 'build me a site for my roofing business' and it does not stop — it produces one, with an invented brand, invented services, invented testimonials, a stack it chose silently, and a purple gradient hero. None of those were rejected; they were never considered. And every later prompt inherits them, so messages two through ten are spent undoing defaults you never picked.
solves: Vague prompts whose real cost is the redo, not a slightly worse site
Invented content — fake testimonials and services — appearing in a client demo
A tech stack chosen silently by the model
Ten follow-up prompts fighting decisions made in prompt one
inside: The decision list — everything a builder will otherwise decide for you, in order
Prompts written from your answers, per page and per section
A content inventory that separates what you have from what must be written
Redo arithmetic: what each unanswered question costs in credits and hours
Guardrails against invented facts, testimonials and statistics
A handover-ready brief for a client or a contractor
outcomes: A first prompt that produces a site worth iterating on
No invented testimonials in anything you show a client
A written brief you can reuse for the next site in ten minutes
usage: Open index.html and work down the decision list before opening any builder.
Fill in the content inventory honestly — what does not exist has to be written by someone.
Generate the prompts and paste the first one whole.
Keep the guardrail lines in every prompt; they are what stop invention.
Save the brief; the next site starts from it.
notFor: Anyone wanting the site built here — it writes the prompts, not the HTML
proof: Nothing here talks to a model. It works out what the model should be told, and prices what leaving it unsaid costs.

name: Local Business Website Studio
tagline: A finished demo site in about ten minutes
oneLiner: Builds a complete one-page site for twelve local trades and exports it as one self-contained HTML file you can hand over or host anywhere.
audience: Anyone selling websites to plumbers, salons, garages and restaurants
Freelancers who pitch with a deck and lose to whoever showed a demo
Local businesses building their own first site
problem: Selling a website to a local business works far better if you show the finished thing instead of describing it — the owner cannot evaluate a proposal but can absolutely evaluate their own shop front. The bottleneck is build time: nobody speculatively builds ten sites, because ten sites is a fortnight.
solves: Pitching a website with a proposal instead of the website
A fortnight of speculative build time you cannot afford
Generic demo copy that does not sound like the trade
Handover that requires hosting, a build step and an explanation
inside: Builder — every field of the site as a form, with live preview at three widths
Twelve trades with demo copy written for each: plumber, electrician, garage, cleaner, landscaper, salon, restaurant, bakery, dentist, gym, accountant, estate agent
Repeaters for services, jobs, testimonials, packages and FAQ, with per-section switches
Palettes and layouts chosen to suit each trade
Export as one self-contained HTML file — no build, no dependencies, no hosting requirement
Handover notes for a non-technical owner
outcomes: Ten demo sites in an afternoon rather than a fortnight
A file the client can host anywhere, or you can host for them
A pitch that opens with the thing rather than a description of it
usage: Open index.html and choose the trade — the demo copy arrives written for it.
Paste the client's real name, phone number, services and areas over the placeholders.
Check the preview at all three widths; local traffic is mostly phones.
Export the single HTML file and show it to the owner.
On acceptance, replace the remaining placeholder content with their real photos and copy.
notFor: Multi-page sites, e-commerce or booking systems
Anyone needing a CMS the client can edit themselves
proof: Demo copy is written for the trade and is not about the specific business. Every claim in it must be replaced with something true before the client publishes.
